reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Measured adoption of AI in educational services is modest and has moved down, not up, in the federal survey that covers it. Per the Census Bureau, the share of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answering Yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks stood at 30.0% in the latest period, against 35.5% in the prior period. The question was first asked in September 2023. That is the only quantitative adoption figure in the material, and it describes firms in the sector rather than schools or classrooms specifically.

The clearest picture of what AI is actually used for comes from the Department of Education, which published an inventory of its own AI use cases alongside federal guidance on innovation and risk management. The listed uses are operational and administrative rather than instructional: real-time transcription and collaboration through Otter.AI, writing feedback and language refinement through Grammarly, and building and scaling applications on foundation models through AWS Bedrock. Other entries describe summarizing documents and extracting action items, generating code snippets in several programming languages including R for data analysis, generating mock datasets for testing, converting data types such as county names into FIPS codes, drafting outreach strategies and project plans, and training employees on prompt engineering. The Department also describes testing filters and data loss prevention methods by feeding AI fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information. CAISY is named as a system for decision-making and operational efficiency through real-time insights, predictive analytics, and intelligent automation.

On money and market structure, the material is thinner. HolonIQ is described as a market-intelligence platform covering the global impact economy, and the site's own description of it says it tracks EdTech funding, digital transformation, and AI learning platforms across K-12, higher education, and workforce learning. HolonIQ's page describes what it offers, sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand, forecasting scenarios, scoring impact, and mapping competitors and partners, and says it serves governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms, and investors. It does not report specific funding totals or vendor market shares in the excerpt available here, so no concentration figure can be stated.

The course catalog material shows where learning supply sits rather than where institutional money goes. The World of AI's catalog lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, with 3 carrying public companion code, each with a verified source and re-verified daily. Ten courses are tracked in the accompanying description, all offering free access to core materials, with three pairing that with a paid certificate option or public code repositories. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry sources including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The catalog notes a structural split: university courses tend to be exam-driven theory while the industry courses are described as code-first or hands-on. It explicitly does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

On ROI, the sources report no measured returns for education. The Department of Education's inventory describes intended effects, reducing costs, boosting productivity, and improving the accuracy of data-driven decisions, but these are stated as purposes of the tools, not as evaluated outcomes. The catalog material likewise reports no completion or outcome data. A reader should treat claims of efficiency gain in this sector as asserted rather than demonstrated by anything in these sources.

The regulatory posture is set at the federal level. The Department of Education frames its guidance around adherence to federal regulations, responsible and secure usage, and risk management, and ties its work to the Executive Order titled Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. The site's own summary of that guidance says it frames permissible use, risk, and procurement for US education. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few plain conclusions: adoption among educational services firms is real but not dominant and recently declined in the survey measure, the documented deployments are concentrated in administration, drafting, transcription, coding, and document review rather than core instruction, and the available guidance emphasizes risk management and procurement discipline rather than speed. The sources do not supply cost benchmarks, vendor pricing, or outcome studies for this sector, so those decisions would rest on evidence outside this material.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
